name: Corvina (Valpolicella)

lines.s10: Corvina is the grape of Valpolicella and Amarone: sour cherry and bitter almond, light and tart, or dried and deep.
lines.s20: Corvina is the main grape of Valpolicella, north of Verona, where fresh it makes a pale, tart red of sour cherry and bitter almond. Dried for months before pressing, the same grapes become Amarone, dark and warming.
lines.s45: Corvina makes a pale, tart red for lunch and a dark, warming Amarone for winter. It is the main grape of Valpolicella, north of Verona. Fermented fresh, it gives sour cherry and cranberry with a bitter almond finish, lively acidity and little tannin. Dried in airy lofts for three or four months, the same grapes make Amarone: raisined black cherry, fig and cinnamon. Pour the young wine cool with charcuterie, and Amarone with braised beef or aged cheese. The story goes that Amarone began as a cask of sweet Recioto, forgotten until it had fermented dry.
lines.sale: With Corvina one grape can carry the whole evening, from a cool, tart red to a dried, deep Amarone. Start with a Valpolicella beside the charcuterie and keep the Amarone for the braised beef or the cheese.

glass.lead: Sour cherry and bitter almond, pale and tart when fresh, with raisined black cherry, fig and cinnamon when the grapes are dried.

ladder.where: The higher hill vineyards, cooled at night by air off the Lessini
The lower, warmer slopes running down towards Verona

glass.structure: Dry. Fresh Valpolicella: acidity high, tannin low, alcohol medium, body light. Amarone: alcohol high, body full, tannin medium, acidity still fresh.

home.home: The hills north of Verona: Valpolicella, where it leads a blend with Rondinella, and Bardolino on Lake Garda. One blend makes four wines by method: fresh Valpolicella, Ripasso refermented on Amarone skins, and Amarone and Recioto from grapes dried for months.
home.abroad: It rarely leaves the Veneto. A few vineyards in Argentina's Andean foothills and in Australia grow it, some of the grapes dried in the Veronese manner.

service.temp: Valpolicella 54 to 59, Amarone 61 to 64 degrees Fahrenheit; 12 to 15 and 16 to 18 degrees Celsius.
service.glass: A standard red wine glass for Valpolicella; a large Burgundy bowl for Amarone.
service.decant: Not for fresh Valpolicella; consider it for a young Amarone, and decant an old one off its sediment.
service.age: Valpolicella young, within two or three years; Amarone ten to twenty years, or more.

with.why: served cool, tart cherry lifts the salt and fat

with.dish: Grilled tuna or salmon, with Bardolino
with.why: a light, low tannin red that spares the fish
raisined fruit and weight match the long braise
salt and crystals beside Amarone's dried fruit

labels.means: From the five historic communes in the west of the zone: fresh, pale and tart.
Valpolicella refermented on the skins left from Amarone or Recioto: fuller and rounder.
Dry red from grapes dried for months, at least 14 per cent alcohol, aged two years at least.
The sweet wine of the same dried grapes, its fermentation stopped with sugar left.
Light Corvina reds from Lake Garda's eastern shore; Chiaretto is the pale rosé.

guest.a: No, it is dry, though rich and warming. Its name comes from amaro, bitter, to set it apart from Recioto, the sweet wine of the same dried grapes.

guest.q: What does Ripasso mean on the label?
guest.a: Passed over again: young Valpolicella is refermented on the skins left from Amarone, which gives it more body, colour and raisined fruit. It sits between the two in weight.
The grapes dry for months and lose about a third of their weight, so the sugar is concentrated. Fermented dry, that sugar gives at least 14 per cent alcohol, usually more.

compare.tell: Gamay matches fresh Valpolicella's pale colour and tart cherry fruit, often with banana; Corvina gives itself away with a bitter almond, cherry stone finish.
Zinfandel shares Amarone's raisined richness and warmth, with blackberry jam and black pepper; Amarone has more sour cherry and a bitter cherry stone finish.
Sangiovese is firmer, with dusty tannin and tomato leaf; fresh Corvina is lighter and softer in grip, with a bitter almond finish.

cards.front: Corvina: which four wines does Valpolicella make from one blend?
cards.back: Valpolicella, fresh; Ripasso, refermented on the skins of dried grapes; Amarone, dry, from dried grapes; and Recioto, sweet, from dried grapes.

cards.front: Corvina for Amarone: how long do the grapes dry, and what do they lose?
cards.back: Three to four months in a drying loft, losing about a third of their weight, which concentrates sugar, acid and glycerol.

cards.front: Corvina blind: what tell do fresh Valpolicella and Amarone share?
cards.back: A bitter almond, cherry stone finish over sour cherry: fresh and pale in Valpolicella, raisined and dense in Amarone.

questions.q: A dry red poured blind is dark and warming, with raisined black cherry, dried fig, cinnamon and a bitter cherry stone finish. Which wine is it?
questions.exp: Dried grape richness with cherry stone bitterness and cinnamon, fermented dry, is Amarone. Recioto, the nearest wrong option, comes from the same dried grapes but is sweet.

questions.q: A guest finds plain Valpolicella too light and Amarone too heavy, and asks for a Corvina red between the two in weight. Which do you suggest?
questions.exp: Ripasso is Valpolicella refermented on the skins left from Amarone, which adds body and raisined fruit. Recioto, the nearest miss, is sweet, and Bardolino is lighter still.

questions.q: A guest reading an Amarone back label asks which grape leads the blend. Which do you name?
questions.exp: Corvina leads at 45 to 95 per cent, and Corvinone may stand in for up to half of it. Rondinella, the nearest miss, is the reliable second grape at 5 to 30 per cent.

report: Mode home, as the plan fixes it. Nothing contradicts TASTE.world old.

The Valpolicella facts (Corvina 45 to 95 per cent with Corvinone standing in for up to half, Rondinella 5 to 30 per cent, the four wines of one blend, the five Classico communes, drying for three to four months with a third of the weight lost, Amarone at least 14 per cent alcohol and two years of ageing, Ripasso on the pomace of Amarone or Recioto, Bardolino and Chiaretto on Garda, the eastern valleys cooler and later) all stand on the Codex's Veneto record.

The story that Amarone began as a cask of Recioto left to ferment dry, and its name from amaro, bitter, set against the sweet Recioto, stand on several trade sources, which disagree on the date of the first labelled bottle and on who named it; the entry calls it a story and gives no date.

Abroad: all but unknown outside north east Italy, with a few growers in Australia (the Australian Wine Research Institute) and a small Andean planting in Argentina, some of it dried (trade sources that name a producer, so not cited). The sites were read through search results only.

The ladder is weak by nature: Corvina is grown in one moderate zone. The cool rung rests on the Codex's own note that the eastern valleys are cooler and later; the notes on each rung are a taster's reading, not a sourced contrast. A checker may prefer to drop to the Classico hills and Bardolino.
Clove in the spice group and prune among the dried fruit are a taster's naming beside the Codex's cinnamon and fig; a checker should weigh them.
The Codex's profile and the Régionale row disagree on acidity (TASTE gives acid 2, INTRO_GRAPES and GRAPES_PLUS high); the structure line says high for fresh Valpolicella, as GRAPES_PLUS does.
The roster name carries Valpolicella in brackets; the spoken lines name Corvina alone, which the lint reads as the grape's name.

checked.verdict: Sound after seven fixes. The Valpolicella blend, the drying and the four wines stand on the Codex; the ladder gave the tart notes to the eastern valleys the Codex knows for dense Amarone, Amarone had no serving figure, two tells parted Corvina by notes the other grape carries, and two small words were brought into line.
changed: glass.ladder.0.where: The cool rung gave the light, tart notes to the eastern valleys, which the Codex's Veneto record calls cooler and later but known for dense Amarone. The rung now names what the record says cools the zone, the night air off the Lessini, on the higher hill vineyards.

glass.ladder.1.where: With the cool rung set by height, the moderate rung is the lower, warmer slopes towards Verona; the Classico hills hold high and low sites both, and the record calls the plain warm.
glass.structure: Moderate is not a word of the structure scale the other entries use; medium.

service.temp: Amarone was given cool room temperature with no figure, and the brief asks for degrees in figures. The full reds row, 61 to 64 degrees Fahrenheit and 16 to 18 degrees Celsius, agrees with the Codex's Veneto record (just below room temperature); Valpolicella keeps the light reds row, which names it.

compare.1.tell: The tell gave Amarone cinnamon as a parting note, and the Zinfandel entry lists cinnamon. Sour cherry and the bitter cherry stone finish part them, as the reviewed profile's confuse has it (more cherry pit).

compare.2.tell: The tell gave fresh Corvina sour cherry as a parting note, and Sangiovese's entry and profile lead with sour cherry. The lighter body, the softer grip and the bitter almond finish part them.
questions.1.opts.2: Bardolino Chiaretto is the older form; the Codex's Veneto record and the Montepulciano entry write Chiaretto di Bardolino.
open: The ladder by height is an inference from the Codex's climate note, not a sourced tasting contrast.
Wine Folly and Wine Insiders are trade pages; the facts they carry stand on the Codex's Veneto record.
The author's report said practically unknown, a word that carries the retired one inside it; it now says all but unknown. The report is not shipped.
